nameStory: The Ten-ridged Whelk gets its name from the prominent ridges or ribs that spiral around its shell - though you might need to count carefully to spot all ten! As a member of the Neptune whelk family, it's named after the Roman god of the sea, fitting for these ocean-dwelling snails.
description: The Ten-ridged Whelk is a large marine snail that lives in the cold waters off New England's coast. Its most striking feature is the tall, spiral shell decorated with raised ridges that wind around from bottom to top. These impressive shells can grow quite large and are prized finds for beachcombers, often washing up empty after storms. This species holds special honor as the official state shell of Massachusetts.

idTips.label: Spiral ridges
idTips.description: Look for prominent raised ribs that spiral around the shell from base to tip - run your finger along them to feel the distinct raised texture

idTips.label: Shell shape
idTips.description: Tall, conical shell that tapers to a pointed spire, resembling an ice cream cone or tower

idTips.label: Shell opening
idTips.description: Large oval opening with smooth edges, often revealing a glossy interior when the shell is empty

idTips.label: Color pattern
idTips.description: Usually pale brown, tan, or grayish-white with darker bands between the ridges

idTips.label: Shell weight
idTips.description: Feels heavy and solid in your hand due to the thick shell walls - much denser than most other beach shells

habitat: Ten-ridged Whelks live in cold, deep waters along New England's coast, typically on sandy or muddy ocean floors. You won't find living specimens in tide pools, but their empty shells frequently wash up on beaches after storms, especially along the Massachusetts and Maine coasts.

seasonality.spring: Beach-washed shells become more common as spring storms churn up the ocean floor. Look for fresh, intact specimens with bright coloration.
seasonality.summer: Living whelks are active in deeper waters during warmer months, but shells continue to wash ashore. Summer beachcombing often yields weathered but still identifiable specimens.
seasonality.fall: Fall storms bring the best shell collecting opportunities as rough seas dislodge shells from deeper waters. This is prime time for finding large, well-preserved specimens.
seasonality.winter: Winter storms can produce exceptional finds, though cold weather limits comfortable beach searching. Shells found now are often the most pristine due to less handling by other collectors.

funFact: Despite being the official state shell of Massachusetts, Ten-ridged Whelks are actually living animals that can grow so large they sometimes prey on other mollusks by drilling holes through their shells with a specialized feeding structure called a radula - essentially turning them into underwater power drills!
confusionNotes: Ten-ridged Whelks are sometimes confused with other large spiral shells, but the combination of prominent spiral ridges and the tall, conical shape sets them apart. Memory trick: 'Ten ridges tall' - count the ridges and notice the tower-like shape.
contextualKnowledge: The Ten-ridged Whelk is sometimes considered the same species as the Northern Neptune (Neptunea lyrata) by some scientists, which can cause confusion in field guides. Both share the common name 'New England Neptune,' but the ten distinct ridges help distinguish this form.
compareHints: As the only Neptune whelk species commonly found in New England waters, the Ten-ridged Whelk is most similar to other large whelks in the true whelk family. However, its prominent spiral ridges and tall, pointed spire distinguish it from the smoother channeled whelks and knobbed whelks that might wash up on the same beaches.
